title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how artificial intelligence in education (AIEd) has been used in higher education from 2016 through 2022. The authors argue that, because AI tools and publications have expanded rapidly, there is a need for an updated synthesis of the field beyond earlier reviews. They ask where the research has been conducted, which academic departments and learner levels it focuses on, who the intended users are, and what kinds of educational applications of AI are most common.

The study uses a PRISMA-based systematic review of 138 peer-reviewed journal articles published in English between 2016 and 2022. The review includes studies involving the use of AI for educational purposes in higher education and excludes editorials, conference papers, and papers about learning AI as a subject rather than using AI to support learning. The authors code study characteristics deductively and identify AI-use categories inductively. Five major application areas emerge: assessment/evaluation, prediction, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning.

The population and context are higher education settings worldwide. Most included studies focus on undergraduate students, with fewer on graduate students; intended users are primarily students, followed by instructors and managers. Research is geographically distributed across 31 countries and six continents, with Asia leading, especially China and Taiwan. Subject domains most often include language learning, computer science, and engineering. The paper is not about secondary students or ChatGPT feedback specifically; rather, it is a broad field-level review of AI in higher education up to the end of 2022.

The main conclusions are that AIEd research in higher education increased sharply in 2021 and 2022, China has overtaken the United States in publication volume, and education faculty now contribute a larger share of the literature than earlier reviews suggested. The review finds that AI is most commonly used to assess or evaluate learning, predict student outcomes, provide assistant-like support, power intelligent tutoring systems, and manage learning data. The authors also identify gaps: limited research in low-income countries, overconcentration in a few disciplines and undergraduate settings, comparatively little work on instructors and managers, and insufficient exploration of newer tools such as ChatGPT, which had not yet appeared in the reviewed studies.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with a clear PRISMA-based method, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled causal estimates for a specific intervention. It is also not directly about secondary students or ChatGPT-generated writing feedback, so it offers only indirect descriptive evidence relevant to the retrieval topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports broad trends in AI in higher education rather than estimating the impact of a specific intervention on learner outcomes. Any implications for ChatGPT feedback, transfer, subgroup effects, or adverse effects are speculative and not supported by direct effect estimates.
